description_en: Devala Hāṭa is a settlement located between Dehīmāṇḍau in the south-east and Goṭhalāpānī in the north-west. Another name for the locality is Gaḍī.The site is constituted of sevenśikharatemples, lined up next to each others on a raised platform. The monuments are all oriented to the north. The temples were restored by the Department of Archaeology at an unknown date, presumably in the early 2010s. This activity is still visible on the monuments, where all stone blocks have received numbers in paint. It appears that weapons (swords and shields) as well as terracotta and metal vessels of various sizes and shapes were discovered inside theśikharas. The discovered artefacts were all placed in a storeroom (BTD0030-008) built between two tempels and even including the smallśikharaBTD0030-001. After 2015 the storeroom was dismantled. The objects' current location is unknow at the moment.According to Loka Nātha Dulal, the temples previously contained statues of Gaṇeśa, Viṣṇu, Bhagavatī, Sūrya and others. These images were worshipped until some of them were stolen (at a yet unknown date) (Dulal 2005: 30).Except for the easternmost temple (BTD0030-001), all temples are built by pairs, with a common platform (except for BTD0030-004 and 005). Their individual dimensions are as follow:- BTD0030-001: 154 x 110 cm- BTD0030-002: 244 x 228 cm (without platform)- BTD0030-003: 240 x 212 cm (without platform)- BTD0030-004: 432 x 290 cm (with platform)- BTD0030-005: 430 x 285 cm (with platform)- BTD0030-006: 258 x 198 cm (without platform)- BTD0030-007: 248 x 190 cm (without platform)- BTD0030-008 (storeroom, dismantled after 2015): 400 x 450 cmBesides the śikhara tempels the site also comprises stone sculptures, all pertaining to Hinduism, and more specifically to Shaivism with one Gaṇeśa (BTD0030-009), Durgā Mahiṣāsuramardini (BTD0030-010), Brahmā (BTD0030-011), Nandi (BTD0030-012) and Umā Maheśvara (BTD0030-014). Finally, their is also the undated inscribed base of a stone sculpture (BTD0030-013).D. R. Sharma estimated that the paleography of the inscription indicates that it was executed during the 13th century (Sharma 2012: 349). The temples follow the same stylistic features as those elaborated in Ajayamerukot (district of Dadeldhura), with no cornerāmalakas(bhūmi-āmalaka) on theśikhara(except on temples 004 and 005). Given the fact that these temples were erected during the second half of the 14th century, it is likely that the monuments in Devala Hāṭa are also dating from this (post-Khaśa Malla) period. The sculptures must date from the same period, i.e. late 14th and 15th century.
references: Sources and references Inscription identification number BTD0030_I_001 Sources Sharma, Dilli Raj. Heritage of Western Nepal. Art and Architecture . Kathmandu: Centre for Nepal and Asian Studies, 2012: 349.

historical_events.event_name: Land grant and installation of a sculpture
historical_events.event_description: The only inscription at the site is found on the broken base of a stone sculpture (BTD0030-013). The inscription is written indevanāgarīscript and contains six lines.D. R. Sharma read the inscription as follows (Sharma 2012: 349):Oṁ śri bahatari ra na ka sri karlla māhā maṇdalika rāni śri yaṃ debi putra śri Garbha deva sutra dhāra ha ra de be na pyādina nena pyādinala deva kāyana pradattam bhumiand translated it as:In Bahatadi (Baitadi), consecration of... mahāmandalika sri... queen's son, Garbha deva, and Hara Deva the architect... has offered land... as for religious merits.
